https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/16/paks.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Péter: Megnyitják a Ráckevei-Soroksári Duna-ág zsilipjét, hogy több víz jusson a Paksi Atomerőműhöz Belföld Nagy Nikoletta Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Emberfeletti munka folyik Paksnál az Atomerőmű két működő turbinájának üzembentartásáért” – írta Magyar Péter Facebookon. Bejelentette, hogy a szakemberek úgy döntöttek: holnap megnyitják a Ráckevei-Soroksári Duna-ág zsilipjét, és ezzel 20 köbméternyi plusz vizet juttatnak a fő Duna-ágba másodpercenként. A miniszterelnök szerint ezzel két centit nyerhetnek Paksnál. Azt is írta, hogy a keddi és a szerdai nap lesz a kritikus, mert addig további 14-15 centis apadás várható, jelenleg 9 centire vagyunk az utolsó előtti turbina ismételt leállításától. „Ez csak akkor lesz elkerülhető, ha a bárkák süllyesztése meghozza a várt eredményt” – tette hozzá. Csütörtöktől aztán az osztrák vízgyűjtőkre érkezik csapadék, amitől újra emelkedhet a vízszint. „Jelenleg is zajlik a két 80 méteres bárka lassú süllyesztése. Még ma estig elérjük az 1 méteres süllyedési szintet, és holnap reggeltől újra indul a víz beszivattyúzása a hajótestekbe” – írta. A miniszterelnök szombat reggeli élő bejelentkezésében megmutatta, hogy két Airbus H255M honvédségi helikopter megkezdte a Dunakilitiről hozott kéttonnás betonkockák beemelését a Dunába. A két 80 méteres bárkát beállították a kijelölt helyükre, irányított süllyesztésük megkezdődött. A kormány még hétközben ismertette, hogyan képzeli el a paksi vízszint megemelését. Az ideiglenesen lehelyezendő bárkák hasonló hatást fognak kiváltani, mint a fenékküszöb, azaz egy kisebb szakaszon lelassítják és felduzzasztják a vizet. Magyar Péter az élőben arról is beszélt két vízügyi szakemberrel, hogy nyolc szivattyúval emelik be a vizet a bárkák belsejébe, illetve a Duna mindkét partján megkezdődött a fenékküszöb kialakítása. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckge.text: Figure caption, What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections By James FitzGerald Â and Â Kayla Epstein Published 1 October 2026 Updated 1 hour ago US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in a critical condition in hospital after Tennessee authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer says. The case of Pike, whose attempted execution on Wednesday had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, raised a number of questions, including what went wrong? And what happens next? A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who has halted executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. How did it go wrong? Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder a year earlier of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike was scheduled to be put to death in Tennessee on Wednesday evening local time. The injections were allowed by the Supreme Court at the 11th hour. Pike was given two injections of the drug pentobarbital, but her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring. Figure caption, Watch: Witnesses recount Christa Pike's failed execution attempt Tennessee halts executions after death row inmate Christa Pike survives hers Published 4 hours ago US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections Published 17 hours ago The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out". The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency. Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have not explained why the dosage given to Pike was non-fatal. Opponents of the death penalty said it was difficult to know what went wrong, because part of Pike's execution happened behind a curtain. Maya Foa, the head of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "Lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life." What happens next? The Tennessee correction department said Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility, while one of her lawyers said on Wednesday that she was being given "life-saving measures" in hospital. On Thursday, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters: "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment." Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine, told the BBC in an email: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she [Pike] will have a brain injury." Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death. In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier. A Supreme Court case from 1947 allowed the state of Louisiana to send Willie Francis, a teenager whose first execution attempt failed when he was 17 years old, back to the electric chair. The court found a second execution would not violate the Constitution's prohibitions against double jeopardy or cruel and unusual punishment and Francis was executed aged 18. "If the question is, is it likely the federal courts would intervene in a second attempt? I'm afraid the answer is a resounding no," Mills said of Pike's case. What is pentobarbital? Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death. Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering". The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods. Why the death penalty is on the rise in US Published 13 August In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes. The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". But the department said in a statement the lethal injection chemical had "consistently been effective". Has this happened before? The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan. The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor. In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Image source, Family handout Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend Who was Colleen Slemmer? Colleen Slemmer's killers met at a job training camp for troubled teens. She was found with an inverted pentagram - a symbol associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull. Colleen's mum, May Martinez, drove 11 hours from Florida to attend the execution, she told People , external , alongside with her husband Raul. She said: "I wanted her [Pike] to remember who Colleen was and what they've done and never forget that thought, no matter where she goes." Shipp was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole and he remains in prison. He was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time. Correction 1 October: This article originally referred to the inmate executed by the state of Louisiana in 1947 as Willie Smith. We have amended the article to make clear that his name was Willie Francis. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Ann Lawani Photograph: Julian Smart/ University of San Francisco View image in fullscreen Ann Lawani Photograph: Julian Smart/ University of San Francisco ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) Calls grow for release of beloved California nurse detained by ICE: ‘We want her home’ Ann Lawani was taken from her home, sparking a huge outcry among students and faculty at her university Uwa Ede-Osifo Thu 12 Nov 2026 19.19 EST Last modified on Thu 12 Nov 2026 19.21 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nearly two months after ICE agents whisked a beloved California nurse and professor from her home in Lodi, her university has ramped up calls for her release. “She needs to come home,” said Eileen Fry-Bowers, dean for the University of San Francisco’s nursing school,in reference to Ann Lawani, who was arrested by immigration agents in September and has since been shuffled between detention centers in California, Texas, and Louisiana, in a series of opaque transfers. Lawani, 39, came to the US in 2007. She established herself as a nursing professional, obtaining a master’s and doctoral degree in the field, before stepping into academia. She steers two programs at the University of San Francisco, one a master’s entry program geared toward students with non-nursing backgrounds and another a bachelor’s program for students seeking to work in public health safety-net institutions. Democrats push to rein in Trump on immigration after voter backlash to ICE raids Read more “She basically has her hands on almost 300 students that she engages with on a regular basis,” Fry-Bowers said. Lawani’s detention has sparked outcry from local lawmakers, who have advocated on her behalf to ICE authorities, as well as her students and colleagues, who say her absence is deeply felt on campus. One of those students, Casey Murray, a nursing science graduate student, described Lawani as a warm educator who could recall the first and last names of pupils she had not seen since orientation. “We have 37 days left until we graduate,” Murray said. “She has supported us to the fullest extent up until the point that she was kidnapped. We want her at our graduation, and we want her home with her family.” Federal immigration officials say Lawani entered the US on a visitor’s visa in 2007, which she overstayed. She was issued a final order of removal in August 2013, according to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson. Natalia Santanna, Lawani’s lawyer, confirmed the removal order, but noted that DHS’s account was “incomplete”. “Dr Lawani applied for asylum within one year of being in the United States. And, in the same 2013 order, the immigration judge found that Ann would more likely than not face persecution in Nigeria and granted withholding of removal,” Santanna said. “That is not a temporary stay. It is a continuing bar to removal to Nigeria. Dr Lawani has lived in the United States pursuant to that grant of withholding of removal since 2013.” Santanna said they have filed a habeas petition to challenge the legality of her detainment, which remains pending in California’s eastern district court. Meanwhile, Lawani’s students and colleagues are continuing to mobilize around her. Lawani sent Fry-Bowers a text about being in ICE’s custody, shortly after her arrest. Fry-Bowers, who was on vacation, heard from another dean that Lawani had been absent from a meeting, which she described as out of character. After the school heard from Lawani’s family, they jumped into action, aiding with legal representation and registering their alarm with the area’s congressional delegation. In late October, Josh Harder, a congressman, who represents Lawani’s district, expressed his concerns about her case to DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin, among them the lack of notice before her arrest and her various whereabouts not being reflected in an online detainee database. “Given her longstanding compliance, lack of criminal history, and substantial community ties, there is no apparent public safety justification for keeping her detained thousands of miles from home while her case proceeds,” Harder wrote then in a letter . Fry-Bowers praised Lawani, citing her work with patients in hospice and palliative care. “She cares for the most vulnerable, helps them maintain their dignity and comfort as they prepare for death,” she said. “She is a consummate professional. The highest praise I could ever give a nursing colleague is that I would want them taking care of my family member or myself, and she would be at the top of the list.” Explore more on these topics ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) California West Coast news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
